_about: One lesson per level (Part 1 of every leaf). See CONTENT_GUIDE.md. id = the level id. photos = photo ids from photos.json. explanation and howToHelp = lists of short lines (each line is shown on its own). howToHelpTitle = optional heading for the howToHelp part. examples = short stories (name, emoji icon, text). askYou = the question in the speech balloon.

explanation: Happy is a good feeling.
We feel happy when something nice happens.
How can you tell?
Look at the face! A happy person smiles.
Their eyes look bright.
They may laugh, jump or play.
howToHelp: Smile back at them.
Play with them and share the fun.
You can say: “I am happy too!”

examples.name: Dina
examples.text: Dina really likes playing ball ⚽. Playing makes her happy!

examples.name: Jim
examples.text: Jim likes eating cookies 🍪. Snacks make him happy.

examples.name: Zib the alien
examples.text: Zib loves looking at the stars ✨. The stars make Zib happy!

explanation: Sad is a heavy feeling.
We feel sad when we lose something, or when we miss someone.
How can you tell?
A sad person may cry.
The corners of their mouth go down.
They may look at the floor, or sit alone.
They may be very quiet.
howToHelp: Sit with them.
Use a soft voice. Ask: “Are you OK?”
You can give a hug, but ask first.
If they keep crying, tell a grown-up.

examples.name: Leo
examples.text: Leo's balloon flew away 🎈. He felt sad and cried a little.

examples.name: Noa
examples.text: Noa's best friend moved to a new town 🏠. Noa misses her. She feels sad.

examples.name: Robo the robot
examples.text: Robo's tower fell down 🧱. Robo felt sad. Then a friend helped him build it again!

explanations.askYou: What makes YOU sad? What helps you feel better?

explanation: Angry is a big, hot feeling.
We feel angry when something is not fair, or when someone hurts us.
How can you tell?
An angry person frowns. Their eyebrows go down.
Their face may go red.
They may shout, stomp, or make fists.
howToHelp: Stay calm. Do not shout back.
Give them some space.
You can say: “Let's take deep breaths together.”
If someone could get hurt, get a grown-up.

examples.name: Ben
examples.text: Someone broke Ben's Lego tower on purpose 🧱. Ben felt angry. His face got hot.

examples.name: Ava
examples.text: Ava had to stop her game 🎮. She felt angry and stomped her feet.

examples.name: Luna the space cat
examples.text: Someone stepped on Luna's tail 🐾. She felt angry. She took deep breaths to calm down.

explanations.askYou: What makes YOU angry? What helps you calm down?

explanation: Tired means our body needs rest.
We feel tired after a long day, or when we did not sleep enough.
How can you tell?
A tired person yawns.
Their eyes close, or they rub their eyes.
They may rest their head on the table.
They move slowly.
howToHelp: Let them rest in a quiet place.
Make the lights soft.
Give them some water or a snack.
Do not ask them to play loud games now.

examples.name: Lily
examples.text: Lily swam all day at the beach 🏊. In the evening she was very tired.

examples.name: Omar
examples.text: Omar went to bed late 🌙. The next day his eyes felt heavy at school.

examples.name: Captain Kai
examples.text: Captain Kai flew the rocket for a long time 🚀. Then Kai needed a nap!

explanations.askYou: When do YOU feel tired? What helps you rest?

explanation: Annoyed is a small angry feeling.
We feel annoyed when something bothers us again and again, like a loud noise.
How can you tell?
An annoyed person may cross their arms.
They may pout, or roll their eyes.
They may sigh, or say: “Stop it!”
howToHelp: Stop the thing that bothers them.
Make it quiet.
Give them some space.
Ask: “What is bothering you?”

examples.name: Max
examples.text: Max's little brother poked him again and again 👉. Max felt annoyed.

examples.name: Dina
examples.text: A mosquito kept buzzing around Dina's head 🦟. She felt annoyed.

examples.name: Zib the alien
examples.text: Zib's radio kept beeping 📻. Beep, beep, beep! Zib felt annoyed.

explanation: Jealous is a mixed-up feeling.
We feel jealous when someone has something we want.
It can feel like sad and angry at the same time.
How can you tell?
You can't always see jealousy on a face.
Look at what is happening: does someone have something the person wants?
A jealous person may frown, sulk, or say: “It's not fair!”
howToHelp: Say it: “I feel jealous.” It's OK to have this feeling.
Ask for a turn: “Can I play next?”
Think of something nice that YOU have.
Be happy for your friend. Your turn will come.
If a friend is jealous: share, or take turns.

examples.name: Sam
examples.text: Sam's friend got a new bike 🚲. Sam wanted one too. He felt jealous.

examples.name: Mia
examples.text: Mia's baby brother got lots of hugs 👶. Mia felt jealous. Then Mom hugged her too!

examples.name: Zib the alien
examples.text: Zib's friend had a shiny star ⭐. Zib felt jealous. So Zib asked: “Can I hold it, please?”

explanations.askYou: Have YOU ever felt jealous? What happened?

explanation: Scared (afraid) is a feeling that tells us: “Be careful!”
Fear helps to keep us safe.
Everyone feels scared sometimes, even grown-ups.
How can you tell?
A scared person's eyes open wide.
Their heart beats fast. Their hands may shake.
They may hide, freeze, cry, or want to run away.
howToHelp: Tell a grown-up you trust: “I feel scared.”
Breathe slowly: smell a flower 🌸 (in through your nose), blow out a candle 🕯️ (out through your mouth).
Hold something soft, like a teddy.
Look around and name 5 things you can see.
Say to yourself: “I am safe. This feeling will pass.”
If a friend is scared: stay close and use a calm voice.

examples.name: Leo
examples.text: Leo is scared of the dark 🌙. A night light helps him feel safe.

examples.name: Noa
examples.text: Noa was scared of the loud thunder ⛈️. She held Dad's hand and counted slowly to 10.

examples.name: Robo the robot
examples.text: Robo was scared before his first space walk 🛰️. Captain Kai told him the plan, step by step. Then Robo felt brave!

explanations.askYou: What makes YOU scared? What helps you feel safe?

explanation: Overstimulation means: TOO MUCH for my brain.
Too loud. Too bright. Too many people. Too many smells.
The brain gets full, like a cup that spills over.
This can happen to anyone. It happens a lot to autistic people. That's OK!
How can you tell?
You may cover your ears or close your eyes.
You may feel hot, shaky, or want to run away.
It is hard to think, talk, or listen.
Some people cry, shout, or need to move a lot.
howToHelp: Go to a quiet place and take a break.
Wear headphones or ear defenders 🎧.
Sunglasses or a hat can help with bright lights 🕶️.
Hold a fidget toy or something soft.
Tell a grown-up: “It's too much!” or show your break card.
Breathe slowly and count to 10.
If a friend is overstimulated: talk less, make it quiet, and don't touch them unless they say yes.

examples.name: Jim
examples.text: The party was very loud 🎉. Jim put on his headphones 🎧 and sat in a quiet room. Then he felt better.

examples.name: Lily
examples.text: The shop had bright lights and lots of people 🛒. It was too much for Lily. She told Mom: “I need a break.”

examples.name: Zib the alien
examples.text: The rocket launch was SO loud 🚀. Zib covered his ears and went to his quiet room on the spaceship.

explanations.askYou: What is too much for YOU? Too loud? Too bright? What helps you?

explanation: An unfamiliar place is a place we have never been to before.
Like a new school, an airport, a hotel, or a new doctor.
New places can feel strange or scary. That's OK!
We don't know what will happen, and there may be new sounds, lights and smells.
The good news: we can get ready!
howToHelp: BEFORE: Look at photos or videos of the new place.
Make a plan: What happens first? Next? Last?
Pack your comfort things: headphones 🎧, a toy, a snack 🍎.
AT THE PLACE: Stay close to your grown-up.
Find a quiet spot for breaks.
Agree on a sign that means: “I need a break.”
AFTER: Rest. You did something brave! ⭐

examples.name: Dina
examples.text: Dina went on a plane for the first time ✈️. She looked at photos of the airport before. On the day, she knew what to expect!

examples.name: Omar
examples.text: Omar went to a new dentist 🦷. Mom showed him the plan: wait, sit in the chair, open wide, go home. It helped!

examples.name: Captain Kai
examples.text: Captain Kai lands on new planets all the time 🪐. Kai always brings a map and a favorite snack.

explanations.askYou: Where would YOU like to go? What would you take with you?

explanation: A special interest is something you LOVE and know a LOT about.
Like dinosaurs 🦕, trains 🚂, space 🚀, animals, maps, or a game.
Many autistic people have special interests. They are a great thing!
Talking about them makes us happy.
But other people may like different things.
How can you tell when it is a bit too much for them?
They look away, or look at their phone.
They say “Mm-hm” or “OK” again and again.
They try to change the topic, or start to walk away.
howToHelp: Talk for a little bit. Then stop and ask: “Do you want to hear more?”
Take turns: ask what THEY like, and listen 👂.
Watch their face: are they smiling and asking questions? Then they are interested!
If they look away or change the topic, that's OK. Save the rest for later.
Find friends who love the same thing. You can talk for a long time with them!

examples.name: Leo
examples.text: Leo knows the names of 100 dinosaurs 🦕! He tells his friend about T. rex, then asks: “What's your favorite animal?”

examples.name: Ava
examples.text: Ava loves trains 🚂. She talked about trains for a long time. Her friend looked at the door. Ava said: “Let's talk about you now!”

examples.name: Robo the robot
examples.text: Robo LOVES planets 🪐. Zib loves planets too, so they talk about them for hours!

explanations.askYou: What is YOUR special interest? Who do you like to tell about it?

explanation: Body language means talking without words.
Our face, hands and body can “say” things.
What do hands say?
👋 Waving = “Hello!” or “Bye!”
👍 Thumbs up = “Good!” or “OK!”
🤷 Shrugging your shoulders = “I don't know.”
👉 Pointing = “Look over there!”
Crossed arms and a frown = “I'm upset” or “No.”
How do we look confident (brave and sure)?
Stand tall, with your shoulders back.
Keep your head up.
Use a clear, calm voice.
howToHelp: You don't have to look into people's eyes. Looking at their nose or forehead is OK too.
Not sure what someone's body means? It's OK to ask: “Are you OK?” or “Do you want to play?”
To feel confident: take a big breath, stand tall, and smile if you want to.
Everyone's body talks a bit differently. That's OK!

examples.name: Noa
examples.text: Noa waved 👋 at her friend across the playground. Her friend waved back. That means: “Hi!”

examples.name: Ben
examples.text: Ben's teacher gave him a thumbs up 👍 after his test. It meant: “Good job!”

examples.name: Luna the space cat
examples.text: Luna stands tall with her tail up 🐾 when she feels confident and happy.

explanations.askYou: How do YOU stand when you feel strong and brave?

explanation: Sarcasm is when someone says the OPPOSITE of what they mean, often as a joke.
Example: it is raining hard 🌧️. Dad says: “Oh great, what lovely weather!”
He does NOT mean the weather is lovely. He is joking!
How can you tell?
The words don't match what is happening.
The voice sounds a bit funny: slow, or extra happy.
The person may smile a little, roll their eyes, or wink 😉.
Sarcasm can be hard to spot. That's OK! Lots of people find it hard.
howToHelp: Check: do the words match what is happening?
Not sure? Ask: “Are you joking?” or “Do you mean that?”
You can say: “Sarcasm is hard for me. Please say it plainly.”
If sarcasm feels mean, you can say: “That hurt my feelings.”
Good friends will explain the joke.

examples.name: Jim
examples.text: Jim dropped his books 📚. His friend smiled and said: “Smooth move!” Jim asked: “Are you joking?” His friend said: “Yes! Let me help you.”

examples.name: Lily
examples.text: It was very hot outside ☀️. Mom said: “Wow, it's SO cold today!” and winked. Lily laughed. Mom was joking!

examples.name: Zib the alien
examples.text: Zib's spaceship was very messy 🚀. Robo said: “Wow, so tidy!” Zib knew it was sarcasm, because the ship was NOT tidy.

explanations.askYou: Has someone said something that did not match what was happening? What did you do?

explanation: A bully is someone who is mean to another person again and again, on purpose.
Bullies may call names, laugh at someone, push, leave someone out, or say mean things online.
Ableism is when people are mean or unfair to someone because they are disabled or different. For example, because they are autistic.
Being autistic is NOT bad. Your brain works in its own way, and that's OK!
If someone is mean to you, it is NOT your fault.
How can you tell it is bullying?
It happens again and again.
It makes you feel scared, sad, or alone.
The other person keeps going when you say stop.
howToHelp: Say in a strong, calm voice: “Stop. I don't like that.”
Walk away to a safe place, near a grown-up.
Tell a grown-up you trust, like a parent or a teacher. Keep telling until someone helps.
Telling is NOT tattling. It keeps you safe.
Stay close to friends who are kind to you.
If you see someone being bullied: don't laugh along. Stand with them, and tell a grown-up.
You deserve to be treated with kindness. 💜

examples.name: Sam
examples.text: Some kids laughed when Sam flapped his hands 🙌. Sam told his teacher. The teacher helped, and the kids stopped.

examples.name: Mia
examples.text: A girl kept calling Mia names. Mia said: “Stop. I don't like that.” Then she walked to her friends and told Mom after school.

examples.name: Robo the robot
examples.text: Some robots said Robo was “weird” because he beeps differently. Zib stood next to him and said: “Robo is my friend. Stop!”

explanations.askYou: Who is a grown-up YOU can tell if someone is mean to you?
